Clerkenwell · Illustration

Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration: beyond the familiar drawings

London’s new home for illustration uses a beautifully restored industrial site to make the case that drawings are not the supporting act. They are the story.

By Paolo Pastorino27 September 20266 min read
At a glance
Where
1 Myddelton Passage, Clerkenwell, EC1R 1AG ↗
Hours
Wednesday–Sunday, 10:00–17:00; last exhibition entry 16:00 ↗
Tickets
Paid exhibitions; concessions and some free activities ↗
Allow
90 minutes to 2 hours

The name above the door may be Quentin Blake’s, but the Centre is not a monument to one illustrator. Its real subject is the restless territory between an idea and an image: picture books, comics, reportage, murals, theatre work and the drawings that never become finished publications.

That breadth is what makes the visit worthwhile. You may arrive expecting the loose ink lines most closely associated with Roald Dahl and leave thinking about illustration as performance, argument or private experiment.

A new use for New River Head

The Centre opened in June 2026 at New River Head in Clerkenwell. The former waterworks buildings give the visit an atmosphere that a neutral white gallery would struggle to create. Brick, courtyards and traces of industry frame the exhibitions without overpowering them.

It is compact enough to understand in one visit but not so small that the ticket feels like an entrance fee for a single room. Alongside the galleries there is a library, a creative studio, a café and a shop. The result feels closer to a working centre than a polished shrine.

Start with Quentin Blake, then keep going

The long-running opening exhibition, Quentin Blake: Performance, brings together more than a hundred original works and looks at the influence of theatre on Blake’s practice. The useful surprise is how quickly the familiar style becomes unfamiliar again. Rough lines that seem spontaneous are shown as the product of timing, movement and repeated decisions.

Do not reduce Blake to his collaborations with Dahl. His hospital commissions, independent books, adult work and experiments with scale show a much wider practice. Seen together, the drawings have the energy of people entering a stage rather than characters waiting obediently on a page.

The other galleries widen the lens. Their exhibitions change, which is exactly why the Centre should not be treated as a one-off destination. Check what is current before travelling, especially if a temporary show is the main reason for your visit.

Look closely, not quickly

Illustration often appears effortless because the final image has already solved its problems. Here, original drawings make hesitation visible: pencil marks beneath ink, changes in posture, empty space doing more work than expected. A framed sheet can reward several minutes, particularly when it sits beside another version of the same idea.

The temptation is to photograph every witty image and move on. Resist it. Choose a handful of drawings and look at how the line controls pace, where the eye enters the page and what has deliberately been left out. The Centre is at its best when it teaches you to read an image with the patience usually reserved for text.

How much time to allow

Allow around 90 minutes for the exhibitions and longer if you plan to use the library, stop at the café or visit with children. The scale makes it easy to combine with the London Canal Museum, Exmouth Market or a walk through Clerkenwell, but cramming it between two larger museums would miss the point.

The building is open Wednesday to Sunday. Exhibition admission is paid, with concessions, while some events and activities are free. Current exhibitions, prices and last-entry times can change, so use the official visit page rather than an old listing.

Who should go

This is an obvious destination for illustrators, designers and families, but that description is too narrow. Anyone interested in how ideas become visible will find something here: the false confidence of a finished line, the comedy of a tiny gesture, or the politics carried by an image before a caption says anything.

The Centre’s best trick is to make a drawing look less simple the longer you spend with it.

Go for Quentin Blake if that is the hook you need. Stay for the evidence that illustration is not decoration around a story; very often, it is the part that tells us how to read it.
